primarySource.title: Analysis of Stand Your Ground Self-defense Laws and Statewide Rates of Homicides and Firearm Homicides

per: adoption of statutory public-place stand-your-ground law versus no such adoption in the controlled pooled study
evidence: researched; observational controlled interrupted time series

chain: The study associates statutory stand-your-ground adoption with higher monthly firearm-homicide rates after controlling for comparison states, seasonality and long-term trends.
Its treatment is an extension of legal immunity for lethal self-defense outside the home to places where a person has a legal right to be.

That legal change can alter the perceived legal consequences of choosing lethal force. The authors describe possible encouragement of otherwise avoidable deadly encounters; deterrence is the competing explanation.

A person chooses whether to use lethal force in a particular encounter from the situation and their own record. A firearm discharge can physically kill another person. The aggregate estimate does not choose that action or victim.
whyDoesThisHappen.terminal: Legal rule: statutory protection for qualifying public-place self-defense; physical fact: lethal force can kill. Actual behavioral mediation is not identified by this study.
whyDoesThisHappen.identifiedVsHypothesized: The legal treatment and aggregate association are measured in the paper. The psychological pathway is an authors-discussed hypothesis, not measured person-level mediation or proof of a particular encounter.

isReverseTrueOnRepeal.reason: The treatment analyzed is adoption during2000–2016; no repeal experiment or repeal estimate is supplied. Prior deaths cannot reverse. Future encounters require the actual replacement law and effective date. Do not negate0.08 or invert1.08 as a researched repeal effect.

whoExactly.studyPopulation: Forty-one US states during1999–2017:23 statutory adopters and18 controls; statewide monthly firearm-homicide deaths per100000people. The dataset includes170659firearm homicides.
whoExactly.exclusions: Nine states excluded:Utah/Iowa lacked sufficient timing/data;seven had case-law stand-your-ground principles, contaminating comparison. No territory, county-specific, township-specific or individual exposed-defendant estimate.
whoExactly.legalCoverage: People in qualifying public-place self-defense encounters under operative law; the study definition is not a grant of authority to local governments or proof every homicide involved a self-defense claim.

howFast.measured: Methods model a step change in monthly statewide rates at statutory enactment, adjusted for seasonality and state trends, with at least12months before/after for included adopters.
howFast.lagInterpretation: lagMonths0 describes that monthly aggregate model specification; it is not a measured immediate personal reaction or zero procedural delay. No separate distributed-lag coefficient is supplied.

doesItDifferByPlace.answer: Yes; the Results section reports substantial state heterogeneity.
doesItDifferByPlace.reported: Large increases in total/firearm homicide associations cluster in several Southern states; reported combined outcome increases16.2%–33.5%. Some states have no statistically significant associations. That combined range is not a firearm-only numerical interval.
doesItDifferByPlace.rangeMeaning: [0.03,0.13] is the published95%interval around the pooled firearm-homicide rate ratio minus1. It is not a distribution of local effects, not a bound on every state, and not a territory transport estimate.
doesItDifferByPlace.exactMissingFigure: Numerical firearm-only state-specific estimates and their intervals fromFigure3/supplement, plus evidence for later-adopting and excluded places. No universal state-specific effect is claimed.

isItReallyAboutZero.answer: No about-zero conclusion for the pooled firearm-homicide association.
isItReallyAboutZero.measured: Main pooled IRR1.08,95%CI1.03–1.13,P=.002. Suicide negative controls are separate outcomes; their near-null results cannot zero firearm homicide.
isItReallyAboutZero.limits: Nonsignificance for a particular state or demographic subgroup does not establish equivalence to zero. Low counts and confounding limit inference. No person-level risk coefficient is supplied.
